name: Free sialic acid storage disease
aliases: infantile free sialic acid storage disease (ISSD)

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by biallelic SLC17A5 variants encoding sialin, the lysosomal membrane transporter that exports free sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) from the lysosome.
The phenotype spans a continuum from the severe infantile form (ISSD) to the milder Salla disease, rather than being two separate diseases.
Infantile sialic acid storage disease presents with fetal hydrops or neonatal ascites, coarse features, hepatosplenomegaly, severe hypotonia, developmental arrest and often early death.

Salla disease, most prevalent in Finnish and Scandinavian populations, presents in infancy with hypotonia, nystagmus and later ataxia, spasticity, intellectual disability and slowly progressive course with longer survival.
Central hypomyelination on brain MRI, with a thin corpus callosum and delayed or deficient myelination, is a characteristic imaging clue.
Diagnosis rests on markedly increased free (unbound) sialic acid excretion in urine and elevated free sialic acid in cultured fibroblasts, confirmed by biallelic SLC17A5 testing.
Distinguish free sialic acid storage (a transporter/storage defect) from sialidosis, which is caused by neuraminidase deficiency and shows raised bound (oligosaccharide-conjugated) sialic acid.
reference.pathophysiology: Free sialic acid storage disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC17A5, encoding sialin, a proton-coupled anionic sugar transporter in the lysosomal membrane. Sialin normally exports free sialic acid, generated by lysosomal degradation of sialoglycoconjugates, from the lysosome to the cytosol. Defective transport causes free sialic acid to accumulate within enlarged, storage-laden lysosomes across many tissues. The nervous system is particularly affected, with impaired and deficient myelination producing the hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy that underlies the hypotonia, nystagmus, ataxia, spasticity and cognitive impairment. Severe alleles that abolish transporter function give the infantile phenotype with widespread visceral storage, hydrops and organomegaly, whereas the recurrent Finnish founder variant retains partial function and produces the comparatively milder, slowly progressive Salla phenotype, illustrating a genotype-severity gradient.
additionalDifferentials: Sialidosis (neuraminidase deficiency) with raised bound sialic acid
GM1/GM2 gangliosidosis and other lysosomal storage disorders
Non-immune hydrops fetalis from other lysosomal storage disorders
Mucopolysaccharidoses with coarse features and organomegaly
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary free sialic acid excretion
Free sialic acid measurement in cultured skin fibroblasts
Biallelic SLC17A5 molecular genetic testing including founder-variant analysis
Brain MRI for hypomyelination and thin corpus callosum
Abdominal imaging for hepatosplenomegaly and, antenatally, hydrops/ascites
Developmental and neurological assessment with ophthalmological review for nystagmus
Enzymatic exclusion of neuraminidase deficiency to differentiate from sialidosis
redFlags: Non-immune fetal hydrops or neonatal ascites with organomegaly
Neonatal severe hypotonia with developmental arrest and coarse features
Progressive spasticity and ataxia with hypomyelination on MRI
Failure to thrive with hepatosplenomegaly in infancy
Nystagmus with global developmental delay in an infant
reference.prognosis: The infantile form carries a poor prognosis with severe neurological impairment and frequently death in early childhood, whereas Salla disease is slowly progressive with intellectual disability and motor impairment but survival often into adulthood. No disease-modifying therapy is available and management is supportive.
pitfalls: Confusing free sialic acid storage disease with sialidosis; the former shows raised free and the latter raised bound sialic acid
Overlooking the diagnosis in unexplained non-immune hydrops fetalis
Attributing hypomyelination solely to more common leukodystrophies without measuring urinary free sialic acid
Assuming a single severe phenotype and missing milder, slowly progressive Salla presentations
Relying on non-specific coarse features and organomegaly without targeted biochemical testing
